No catalog record for lala1270. Full text not read.
new_statements.rule_in_words: No placement rule is recoverable. What is visible: Rensch treats the ballistic/controlled opposition as a property of stressed syllables ('In Chinantec it occurs only in stressed syllables'; Amuzgo has it in stressed or unstressed syllables), independent of vowel length in Lalana, with tone allophony described for 'controlled stressed syllables'. Where the stressed syllable falls in the word is not stated in any snippet.
new_statements.identity_note: All four works concern Lalana Chinantec (cnl; Rensch's fieldwork variety, San Juan Lalana, Oaxaca); Rensch 1978 also treats Guerrero Amuzgo and other Otomanguean languages, Rensch 1968 all Chinantec varieties (Lalana = sec. 1.11).

new_statements.relation_note: The language is not in the catalog; the only existing statement is an empty pointer to Rensch 1978 Table 28. Mugele 1982 supplies the actual content: it adopts Rensch's (1978) term 'stressed syllable' = Full (stem) syllable, states the Full/Restricted distribution (stem vs affix; final syllable of disyllabic stems), and confines the ballistic/controlled contrast to stressed syllables. Compatible with Rensch 1978 (which Mugele cites as the source of the usage) and with the outside summaries logged earlier (Yip 2002 'stress is on the final syllable'; Oxford Handbook Table 28.6 'controlled stress / ballistic stress' from Mugele 1982:9).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Lalana Chinantec is a tone language (7 tones plus a ballistic/controlled syllable contrast). Word stress is not an independent lexical contrast: the 'stressed syllable' is the Full syllable, which is the stem syllable of the word; affixes, clitics and particles are Restricted (unstressed) syllables with reduced inventories (no long vowels, no nasal contrast, no clusters, no ballistic syllables, no coda /n/, fewer vowels and tones). Stems are almost all monosyllabic; in the rare disyllabic stems the final syllable is the Full (stressed) one. Prefix strings before the stem are unstressed (sec. 4.3.4: 'a sequence of unstressed syllables that precede a stressed syllable'; tone harmony applies only in these). Ch. 4 n. 2: 'ballistic syllables never occur in unstressed syllables.' Historically (p. 145) 'The disyllabic stems of POM were evidently stressed on the second syllable.' Net effect: stress on the stem syllable, which is word-final relative to prefixes (Yip 2002's summary 'stress is on the final syllable' is a restatement of this).
new_statements.secondary_stress: None described. Mugele notes (p. 10-11, quoting Merrifield 1963:15) that the ballistic/controlled contrast could alternatively have been described as primary vs secondary stress, and (ch. 6 n. 2) that Merrifield's 'stress' means ballistic vs controlled; Mugele himself treats ballistic quality as a syllable feature within stressed (Full) syllables, not as a stress degree.
new_statements.exceptions: Rare disyllabic stems: first syllable Restricted, final syllable Full. Some apparent prefixes may be reduced stems in compounds, 'phonologically reduced when not in the stressed syllable' (p. 122). Ballistic/controlled contrast is restricted to Full syllables bearing High, Low or Falling tone and absent in glottal-stop-checked syllables (p. 9).
new_statements.identity_note: Mugele 1982 describes Lalana Chinantec (LC) as spoken in the municipio of San Juan Lalana, Oaxaca (SIL fieldwork tradition of Rensch); no sub-dialect distinguished. Comparative remarks on Palantla, Tepetotutla, etc. and on Proto-Chinantec/Proto-Otomanguean (p. 145) are about other varieties/stages and were not used for the reading.

sources.note: Comparative only. Proto-Chinantec prosodic elements are two tones *H, *L (combinations HL, LH, HLH) and a 'ballistic accent' that 'could occur with both tones and all three combinations' (p. 12); Lalana (Ll) is said to have lost length in accented syllables closed by *? (p. 13). No statement on word-stress placement in any daughter language. downloaded from an Internet Archive copy of the SIL file (SIL file host could not be reached by automated download here).

sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.note: Silent on stress. Morphophonemics of verb stems (vowel shifts, palatalization). Note 2 (p. 37) restates the Rensch & Rensch 1966 phoneme inventory: prosody phonemes = vowel length, vowel nasalization, tone (1 high, 2 mid, 3 low), plus post-vocalic h reanalysed as the prosodic feature 'ballistic syllable' (marked by acute accent); stress is not mentioned anywhere in the 38 pages (a full-text search for stress/accent scanned for stress/accent/prominence).
